messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina was 21, single, and in her first serious post-training role as a surgeon when the cyclone hit the coastal city where she had been living and working. She had been on call overnight in the hospital when the power failed and the building began to shake with the force of the wind. Water drove sideways against the windows, alarms sounded in overlapping bursts, and the corridor outside the operating suite filled with smoke and shouting as parts of the electrical system gave out. For hours she moved between patients on a dim emergency generator, trying to keep composure while staff and families waited for news that she could not give them. By morning, roads were blocked, the neighborhood around her apartment was flooded, and she learned that a colleague’s car had been swept into a ditch during the evacuation. In the days afterward, Amina began to react intensely to trauma-related events of any kind: hearing flood warnings, seeing disaster footage, or even being asked to revisit that night at work left her tense and withdrawn. She also found that similar weather conditions, especially heavy rain, wind, or the oppressive air before a storm, made her body brace as if the water were coming back. Nighttime was worse still; waking in the dark or hearing the building settle in the small hours brought back the same dread she felt when the hospital lights had gone out.

From the start she came to believe that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, that she could not rely on herself, and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. Those thoughts grew sharper each time she was caught off guard. A siren outside the hospital, the slam of a metal door, or the sudden bark of a monitor beep made her jump harder than other people around her, and she noticed her own body reacting before her mind could catch up—her chest tightening, her stomach dropping, her hands going cold when something reminded her of that night. The more hyperalert she became, scanning hallways, weather reports, and ceiling lights for the next danger, the more certain she felt that she had to protect herself by staying controlled and agreeable. At work she became unusually compliant with senior staff, saying yes when she wanted to ask for help, smoothing over disagreements, and keeping her own distress out of sight. She also stopped exercising, even though she had once gone running after long shifts, because her elevated heart rate and breathlessness felt too much like the physical reactions she feared; what had been a release became something she avoided almost automatically. Yet the effort to control her emotions and make herself smaller did not settle her. It left her feeling even less confident in her own judgment, more convinced that she could not rely on herself to manage what was happening, and more trapped in the belief that the trauma had taken over her life.

That fear, in turn, made the world feel newly dangerous. A dark corridor after a late case, an overcast sky building over the hospital parking lot, or a weather alert on a phone could pull her back into the same sense of threat and make her startle at ordinary sounds again. Once her body was on edge, she watched the environment more closely, and the watching itself seemed to confirm that danger was everywhere. She found herself asking junior staff to walk with her to her car, checking exits before entering a room, and avoiding exercise because anything that raised her pulse made her feel exposed. She understood these habits as necessary, even polite in the case of fawning over others, but they kept her attention fixed on possible disaster and made her more alert to every creak, bang, and sudden movement. That heightened watchfulness then fed the same thoughts she dreaded: if she was always braced, then something must indeed be about to happen, and if she was constantly on guard yet still felt afraid, that seemed to prove she could not trust herself.

As weeks turned into months, Amina’s daily life narrowed around these reactions. She remained outwardly capable in the operating room, but she was spending more energy on monitoring the weather, bracing at sounds, and regulating her face and voice than on recovering her sense of safety. She finally sought help after waking in the dark during a stormy night, heart pounding from a distant crash of thunder, and realizing she had spent the entire shift before that trying to suppress her fear while feeling increasingly certain that she was no longer herself. What she most feared was that another sudden disaster would catch her unprepared and prove her right; what she most hoped for was to feel able to trust her own mind and body again.
